newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower, led by PGMs.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower, led by PGMs.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower Friday, led by profit taking in platinum group metals (PGMs) and liquidation in NYMEX June palladium, ahead of first notice day Monday, traders said.

"With gold and silver struggling a little of late, it was not too surprising that they weakened when the white metals sold off sharply today," said Scott Meyers, senior analyst with Pioneer Futures in New York.
"The news about the Russians resuming PGM exports again soon has been making the market nervous, liquidiation of June palladium long positions was also a factor," he said.

NYMEX June palladium ended down $20.90 an ounce at $172.35, after seeing a contract high at $205.00 an ounce earlier this week, and reducing the June/September backwardation to near zero from a high around $25.00.
NYMEX September palladium lost $12.00 to $173.00 an ounce, but the September/December spread remained in backwardation, reflecting ongoing fears of physical market tightness.
In the bullion market, one month palladium lease rates fell to around 20-30 percent, from near 50 percent Thursday.
In news Thursday, Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, reiterated statements made earlier this month that Russian PGM exports would resume in the next few weeks.

And Japanese traders said Friday representatives from Russia's central bank were expected to visit Japan on June 9 and a visit by Almaz officials was set for June 1 - June 11 to discuss a new PGM supply contract.

Japan is one of the biggest consumers of palladium and Russia supplied 4.6 million ounces out of the world's consumption of 6.8 million ounces in 1996, according to a report by refiners Johnson Matthey earlier this month.

But fiscal and administrative problems in Russia, and a possible change of marketing strategy, have seen Russian exports halted since last December, forcing a run down in world inventories and a surge in the palladium price to 17 year highs.
In addition, U.S. fund Tiger Management is believed to have built up a position of about 1.5 million ounces of palladium in the physical market in recent months.

The fund had not yet sold any of its stockpile, believing Russian supplies will be significantly lower in 1997 than in 1996, while automotive demand for palladium is rising, sources close to the fund said Friday.
Meanwhile, NYMEX July platinum ended down $9.10 an ounce at $401.20, after seeing a contract high at $420.50 earlier this week.

The July/October backwardation narrowed to $3.00 an ounce from over $8.00 an ounce earlier this week, while the October NYMEX platinum/October gold spread slipped to $48.10 an ounce from a contract high at $52.60 earlier this week.
COMEX August gold ended down $1.10 at $347.50 an ounce, after seeing a ten-day intraday high at $350.40 early.
Estimated total COMEX gold volume was 42,000 lots.

Funds were net short 30,237 lots in COMEX gold in the latest CFTC Commitment of Traders data on May 20, but had been seen covering some short positions this week, as gold prices recovered some ground on news of the threat to European Monetary Union posed by the Bundesbank's opposition to the German government plan to revalue its gold reserves.
COMEX gold open interest fell 8,181 lots to 153,869 contracts Thursday, analysts noted. Monday is first notice day for COMEX June gold.

But short positions in the OTC market are believed to remain two or three times larger than the short positions on COMEX as hedge work the "gold-carry trade", borrowing gold at cheap rates to fund investments in dollar-denominated assets, analysts said.
In the bullion market spot gold ended quoted $344.40/90 an ounce, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $345.60 and the New York close Thursday around $345.50/00.
COMEX July silver ended down 16.3 cents at $4.675 an ounce, giving back the week's gains.

But gold and silver were still likely to receive some support from the uncertainty about EMU created by the Bundesbank's opposition to German Finance Minister Waigel's plan to revalue its gold and book the profits to help Germany meet EMU criteria.
Bundesbank gold reserves total about 95 million ounces valued in the books at 144 marks per ounce against a market value of 600 marks.

Marking the reserves to market would produce a revaluation of 40 billion marks ($24 billion), of which about 20 billion marks would be transferred to the government's accounts to reduce Germany's debt to GDP ratio.
Under the Maastricht Treaty, to qualify for EMU, European countries must reduce their debt to 60 percent of GDP.

But in addition Waigel has proposed taking a portion of the revaluation as a part of Bundesbank profits in 1997 and 1998 and classifying it as government revenue to help Germany meet the EMU budget deficit requirement.
To meet EMU criteria, EU fiscal deficits must be reduced to three percent of GDP.
Under EU accounting rules, one off assets sales may be used to the EMU debt-to-GDP criteria, but are not admissable as revenue to reduce the government's budget deficit.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
